newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa to object to proposed EU ostrich ban.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa to object to proposed EU ostrich ban.

text.p: A European Union veterinary committee has proposed a ban on the imports of ostrich meat and live ostriches from South Africa over fears that a deadly human disease can be transmitted via ostrich meat, South African health officials said on Thursday.
The agriculture department said it would object to the proposed blanket ban because a recent outbreak of Congo fever was restricted to just one of South Africa's ostrich abattoirs.
Up to 17 people working at the abattoir are feared to have contracted the tick-borne disease. One of them has died.

Congo-Crimean haemorrhagic fever is an infectious disease that, like the more notorious viral disease Ebola, causes body organs to degenerate with massive internal and some external bleeding. About 30 percent of Congo fever cases are fatal.
South African exports of ostrich meat and products are worth millions of rands each year and accounts for some 85 percent of the world market.

The agriculture department said it understood the EU's standing veterinary committee had recommended the ban to the organisation's College of Commissioners as a precaution, due to uncertainty about the safety of ostrich meat for human consumption in the event of an outbreak of Congo fever.

The department said South Africa had undertaken to conduct urgent research to clarify uncertainties over ostrich meat while the EU had agreed to review its stance once scientific evidence confirmed the disease could not be spread through ostrich meat.
But South Africa would object to a ban on the whole country.
"The ostrich market is highly dependent on the export market," the department said in a statement.

"An official objection will be submitted to the EU requesting the reasons for extending the ban to the total ostrich industry in South Africa, bearing in mind that the recent outbreak was confined to one abattoir only," it said.
South Africa exports more than 400 million rand ($85 million) worth of ostrich leather and 16 million tonnes of ostrich meat worth 58 million rand annually, according to the agriculture department.
South Africa's first confirmed case of Congo fever was in 1981 in a boy bitten by a tick and since then there have been sporadic cases, mainly in rural areas.
